scenes.narration: Nvidia just reported one hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars of revenue in three months. That's more than double a year ago. And at the close on November seventeenth, twenty twenty-six, just before that report came out, the whole company was worth about three point seven five trillion dollars. That's one hundred and fifty-five dollars and forty-six cents a share, times about twenty-four point one billion shares. By our math, that's about sixteen and a half times its profit over the last twelve months.

And that price had just fallen about twenty-two percent in two weeks, from two hundred dollars and thirteen cents on November fourth. In the middle of those two weeks, on November eleventh, the board accepted the resignation of Nvidia's co-founder and C E O, Jensen Huang, after thirty-three years at the top.
So the business is growing faster than ever, yet the multiple is modest. What is that price actually betting on? What has to happen for it to make sense? And what could break the story?
In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Nvidia reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Nvidia's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.narration: First, the machine. Nvidia hasn't filed its full quarterly report yet, so these numbers come from the results it filed with the S E C tonight. Of that one hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars, data centers brought in one hundred and seven point six billion dollars. That's ninety-three percent of everything. The rest, PCs, workstations, cars and robots, now called edge computing, was eight point two billion dollars.

Inside data centers, there are two pipes. The giant cloud companies bought sixty point one billion dollars, up seventy-one percent in a year. The second pipe is AI clouds, industry and enterprise, the newer rental clouds, companies and governments. It brought in forty-seven and a half billion dollars, up a hundred and ninety-five percent. And the new Vera Rubin racks started shipping, in what Nvidia calls the fastest product ramp in its history.

Now the part that makes this machine unusual. Gross margin was seventy-four point eight percent. Operating expenses were only nine point two billion dollars. So operating income came to seventy-seven and a half billion dollars, about sixty-seven percent of revenue, by our math. Net income was sixty-five point three billion dollars, or two dollars and seventy cents a share.

Who pays for all this? By where customers are headquartered, the United States brought in seventy-two point nine billion dollars last quarter, Taiwan thirty point three billion dollars, and China about eleven billion dollars. And it's concentrated. Just three direct customers made up fourteen percent, eleven percent each. That's thirty-six percent of revenue from three buyers, and Nvidia doesn't name them.

Let me draw the machine. Here is the data center pipe, ninety-three percent of the flow. Here is edge computing, the small one. Both pour into this profit box, and look how little leaks out on the way. About two thirds of every dollar of revenue ends up as operating profit.

scenes.narration: A machine this profitable throws off a lot of cash. So where does it go?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Last quarter, operating cash flow was forty-eight point three billion dollars, double the quarter before, partly because of the timing of tax payments. Free cash flow was forty-three point eight billion dollars. Over the last twelve months, by our math, free cash flow was about one hundred and forty-nine billion dollars. And spending on buildings and equipment was only about ten billion dollars. Nvidia designs the chips. Other companies build them.

Then it hands a lot of it back. Last quarter, Nvidia returned twenty-eight point one billion dollars. twenty-two point one billion dollars in buybacks, and six billion dollars in dividends. That's about two thirds of the quarter's free cash. The dividend is now twenty-five cents a share every quarter, up from one cent paid in April. And there's about two hundred and twenty-seven billion dollars of buyback authorization left, which Nvidia plans to use by the end of next fiscal year. That's about six percent of the company's market value, our math.

A footnote on that cash. Customers owe Nvidia eighty-one billion dollars. It now takes sixty-four days on average to get paid, up from sixty. Nvidia says that's partly extended payment terms on big multi-quarter deals. And inventory jumped to thirty-nine point seven billion dollars, from thirty-one point six billion dollars three months earlier, to feed the Rubin ramp.

One more pile. Nvidia holds stakes in other companies worth about one hundred and ten billion dollars, mostly private A I labs and data center financiers. That makes profit lumpy. Over the first nine months of this year, gains on those stakes added twenty-five and a half billion dollars before tax. And last quarter, Nvidia wrote down one point eight billion dollars of private stakes.

scenes.narration: Here's our math, with every assumption on screen. Three lenses. Price to earnings is about sixteen and a half times, or about eighteen point seven times if you strip out the gains on those stakes. Free cash flow yield is about four percent. Operating cash flow yield is about four point two percent. Capital spending is only about six percent of operating cash, so free cash flow is a fair base for the gauge.

Now the reverse calculation. We ask, how fast does free cash flow have to grow for ten years, and then three percent a year forever, to justify today's price? With an eight percent discount rate, the answer is about five and a half percent a year. With ten percent, about ten percent a year. That's our illustration, not a valuation.

Flip it around. If free cash flow never grew at all, the same math says the company would be worth about two point four trillion dollars at eight percent, or about one point eight trillion dollars at ten. So between a third and a half of today's price is a bet on growth.
Here is what flat cash is worth at ten percent. Here it is at eight. And here is the actual price before the report. That gap is the growth you're paying for in advance.

scenes.narration: And here's the strange part. Revenue just grew a hundred and three percent in a year. Nvidia's own outlook for next quarter is one hundred and thirty billion dollars, plus or minus three percent, about twelve percent more than last quarter, with an extra week in it. But the price only asks for five to ten percent a year. So the market isn't paying for today's speed. It's treating this as a peak, and asking whether the cash holds up after the boom.

scenes.narration: So what has to go right?

keyframes.cue: So what has to go right

scenes.narration: One. The big buyers keep building. The giant clouds alone spent sixty point one billion dollars with Nvidia last quarter, and three direct customers were more than a third of revenue. If even one of them slows down, it shows up right away.

Two. Margins hold through the new chips. Nvidia's own outlook calls for gross margin between seventy-one and seventy-two percent next quarter, down from seventy-four point eight percent, as Rubin ramps. A new generation usually starts at lower margins. The question is whether it climbs back.

Three. Customers can pay. Two direct customers account for eighteen and seventeen percent of what Nvidia is owed. And Nvidia now helps some customers finance the build. Its neocloud agreements, up to thirty-two billion dollars, take effect only if those clouds find financing. Its guarantees could reach one hundred and eighteen billion dollars, mostly up to one hundred and five billion dollars of credit support for a giant site in Ohio leased to Open A I. Nvidia says it hasn't paid anything on its guarantees so far.

Four. The supply bet pays off. Nvidia's supply commitments jumped to three hundred and ninety billion dollars, from two hundred and seventy-nine billion dollars a quarter earlier, mostly memory, locked in for years. All its commitments together are five hundred and eighteen billion dollars. By our math, that's about one and a half times its revenue over the last twelve months. Great if demand holds. Heavy if it doesn't.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one, leadership. The C F O, Colette Kress, is now also interim C E O, and the board is searching for a permanent one, inside and outside the company. Harvey Jones became the first chair of the board. The filing doesn't give a reason for the resignation. And in its results, Nvidia lists the leadership transition, and an ongoing investigation by an independent committee of its board, among its risks, without giving details.

Risk two, China. Nvidia shipped two point four billion dollars of older Hopper data center chips to China last quarter. But its outlook for next quarter assumes zero data center compute revenue from China. So China is a swing factor outside the forecast, in both directions.

keyframes.cue: So China is a swing factor
keyframes.label: items[3].at.cue

scenes.narration: Risk three, the web of bets. Stakes of about one hundred and ten billion dollars, guarantees, financing deals, and customers that are also partners. In a boom, these loops help each other. In a slowdown, they could hit revenue, profit and the balance sheet at once.

And the upside the price may not include? Nvidia now sells its Vera C P Us on their own. It agreed to buy Hugging Face, the open A I model platform. Edge computing grew forty-two percent in a year, from workstations to robots and cars. And some neocloud deals give Nvidia a share of their revenue. None of that comes with a dollar figure, so we don't put one on it.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected around late February twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, revenue against Nvidia's own outlook of one hundred and thirty billion dollars, and remember the extra week. Two, gross margin against between seventy-one and seventy-two percent. Three, the days it takes to get paid, against sixty-four days. If those hold, the cash keeps coming, and the price's modest assumption looks easy to meet. If they crack, it means the peak the market already fears has arrived.
That's Nvidia, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
